ch02 - Hit the Lights.md
ch03 - On Through the Never.md
ch04 - Whisper Things Into My Brain Metallica, Emotion, and Morality.md
chapters.relation: Robert Fudge weighs whether Metallica's emotionally violent music corrupts or improves moral character. Against Plato's banishment of passion-stirring art (anger in 'Enter Sandman', indignation in '. . . And Justice for All'), he uses Aristotle's catharsis and the golden mean of healthy anger: 'One' purges pity and fear, and Hetfield's 'St. Anger' purged the rage behind his alcoholism. He then extends Adam Smith's empathy-based account - imaginative placement in the landmine victim's or addict's position - to argue the songs refine moral judgment, even making us question Kant's absolute duty against suicide by confronting the case where the body is a 'holding cell'.

chapters.file: ch05 - This Search Goes On Christian, Warrior, Buddhist.md
chapters.relation: William Irwin traces Hetfield's journey through three sets of virtues: rejecting the Christian virtues of his Christian Science upbringing ('The God That Failed' as Nietzschean slave morality and Marx's opium of the masses), adopting the warrior virtues of Kill 'Em All (life as Hobbesian war, Nietzsche's will to power and 'no remorse'), and finally embracing Buddhist virtues on St. Anger. The warrior code fails without stoicism and collapses into addiction and despair, while the four noble truths - suffering caused by craving ('Frantic', 'Sweet Amber') - fit Hetfield's recovery and growing compassion.

chapters.file: ch06 - Alcoholica When Sweet Amber Becomes the Master of Puppets.md
chapters.relation: Bart Engelen reads 'Master of Puppets' and Hetfield's alcoholism as a case study in akrasia: the Socratic paradox from Plato's Protagoras, Plato's divided soul from the Republic, and Aristotle's weak-willed agent who knows the good but cannot act on it all describe the addict's 'struggle within'. Using Frankfurt's distinction between first- and second-order desires, he argues Hetfield became an 'unwilling addict' - and genuinely irrational - only when he stopped endorsing his desire to drink, and that recovery works through pre-commitment strategies like rehab, avoiding drinking cues, and relying on others.

chapters.file: ch07 - Through the Mist and the Madness Metallica's Message of Nonconformity, Individuality, and Truth.md
chapters.relation: Thomas Nys argues Metallica's early message of nonconformity and individuality ('Metal Militia', 'Motorbreath') converges with Mill's On Liberty: conformity withers human capacities and breeds a stagnant society. Mill's higher pleasures and Nozick's experience machine show why real happiness requires autonomy and earned achievement rather than passive pleasure - the point of 'Escape''s 'Life's for my own to live my own way'. He reads 'Leper Messiah' and 'Eye of the Beholder' as Metallica's versions of Mill's defense of free inquiry and truth against mindless conformity and censorship.

chapters.file: ch08 - Existensica Metallica Meets Existentialism.md
ch09 - The Metal Militia and the Existentialist Club.md
chapters.relation: Jeremy Wisnewski claims Metallica is an existentialist band: Kill 'Em All answers Camus' absurd by creating meaning through chosen, expressive projects ('Metal Militia', 'Motorbreath'), Ride the Lightning's catalogue of deaths ('Fight Fire with Fire' to 'Fade to Black') individualizes us in the Heideggerian confrontation with our own death, and Master of Puppets dramatizes Sartrean bad faith - the 'Sanitarium' label, the soldier as 'Disposable Hero', the addict's lost freedom. He concludes that accusing Metallica of selling out with the Black Album is itself bad faith, since authenticity has no fixed content.

chapters.file: ch10 - The Struggle Within Hetfield, Kierkegaard, and the Pursuit of Authenticity.md
chapters.relation: Philip Lindholm reads Metallica through Kierkegaard's demand for subjectivity: the soldier in 'One' crying 'Oh please God help me' exemplifies becoming a single individual before God against the untruth of the crowd, and 'The Struggle Within' stages Either/Or's passionate choice that decides the self. He then shows Hetfield himself living the inauthentic masked life Kierkegaard condemns - 'I was James Hetfield of Metallica' - until rehab forced the honest self-disclosure ('The God That Failed' and 'Until It Sleeps' mourning his parents) that marks a move toward authentic individuality.

chapters.file: ch11 - Metallica, Nietzsche, and Marx The Immorality of Morality.md
chapters.relation: Peter Fosl argues Metallica's moral critique of religion in 'Leper Messiah' and 'The God That Failed' continues Nietzsche's genealogy of Christian slave morality born of ressentiment and Marx's 'opium of the people': religion gathers a docile herd, denies this world, and exercises power through sin and forgiveness. He diagnoses the band as often stuck in Nietzsche's incomplete nihilism - 'To Live is to Die' longs nostalgically for the Kingdom of Salvation - while 'Escape' and the sheer creative power of the music show a genuine Nietzschean transvaluation and overcoming of Christianity.

chapters.file: ch12 - Metallica's Existential Freedom From We to I and Back Again.md
chapters.relation: Rachael Sotos reads Metallica's career as an existentialist quest for authentic freedom: the Arendtian shared 'we' of the early speed-metal community (Kill 'Em All), the Heideggerian 'I' attuned to death that breaks from das Man (Ride the Lightning's 'Fade to Black'), and the Kierkegaardian leap out of the over-technical system of . . . And Justice for All - compared to Kierkegaard's critique of Hegel - into the embodied groove of the Black Album. Sartre's bad faith explains the rock-star traps, and Some Kind of Monster shows the 'we' must be tended: therapy and a democratic band restore Arendtian public freedom.

chapters.file: ch13 - Living and Dying, Laughing and Crying.md
ch14 - To Live is to Die Metallica and the Meaning of Life.md
chapters.relation: Scott Calef argues Metallica holds there is no meaning of life: the universe is 'much too big to see' ('Through the Never'), Socratic and Schopenhauerian arguments show pleasure, wealth and fame bring only 'King Nothing', and religion is a dishonest Freudian wish-illusion ('The God That Failed') that alienates us from this world. Precisely because life has no objective meaning, Sartre's existence-precedes-essence applies: like Hetfield in his rehab 'confession' and the hunter of 'Of Wolf and Man', we must honestly create meaning by living in the now, with death making life precious rather than pointless.

chapters.file: ch15 - Madness in the Mirror of Reason Metallica and Foucault on Insanity and Confinement.md
chapters.relation: Brian Cameron reads 'Welcome Home (Sanitarium)' and 'Frayed Ends of Sanity' through Foucault's Madness and Civilization: the sanitarium is a total institution whose surveillance and power-knowledge produce docile bodies, confining madness as a threat to the rule of reason just as the seventeenth-century Hopital General confined the idle. Madness is not a mere disease but a socially defined deviance - and a form of rebellion against conformist society - whose violent 'cure' ('violent use brings violent plans') exacts an existential cost on the rebel, as 'The Unforgiven''s bitter old man shows.

chapters.file: ch16 - Ride the Lightning Why Not Execute Killers.md
chapters.relation: Thom Brooks uses 'Ride the Lightning' - the condemned man in the electric chair pleading 'Who made you God to say / I'll take your life from you!' - to examine capital punishment. He presents Kantian retributivism (execution as the only proportional punishment for murder) and then argues against it: the condemned 'dies twice', living for years under a ritualized death sentence that Glover calls cruel, deterrence fails (the brutalization effect), and public justice must not become private vengeance - so even the guilty prisoner in the song is right that we have no right to kill him.

chapters.file: ch17 - Living and Dying as One Suffering and the Ethics of Euthanasia.md
chapters.relation: Jason Eberl uses Joe Bonham of 'One' and Johnny Got His Gun to analyze suffering as loss of recognition (Hegel), loss of social contact (Aristotle's political animal), and loss of Kantian autonomy and dignity - 'a piece of meat that keeps on living'. He then works through the euthanasia debate: active versus passive euthanasia, Aquinas' doctrine of double effect for palliative care, Locke's psychological criterion of personal identity behind the higher-brain death standard applied to Terri Schiavo and PVS patients, concluding that the nurse's cutting of Joe's breathing tube would be active euthanasia because of the intention behind it.

chapters.file: ch18 - Fade to Black Absurdity, Suicide, and the Downward Spiral.md
chapters.relation: Justin Donhauser and Kimberly Blessing read 'Fade to Black' as a meditation on suicide. Against the Schopenhauerian pessimism that life is a downward spiral 'to the musty stench of corpses' - where suicide paradoxically affirms the Will-to-life - they set Camus' absurd: the narrator who loses the will to live surrenders, while Camus' absurd hero lives in revolt, freedom, and passion. Since Schopenhauer and Camus both reject suicide as escape, and Hetfield insists 'writing is therapy', the song's effect is Aristotelian catharsis - purging despair - rather than an endorsement of suicide.

chapters.file: ch19 - Metaphysica, Epistemologica, Metallica.md
ch20 - Believer, Deceiver Metallica, Perception, and Reality.md
chapters.relation: Robert Arp uses Hetfield's lyrics about lies, deception and misperception ('Bad Seed', 'The House Jack Built''s 'Is that the moon or just the light that lights this dead end street?') to stage the perception-reality problem: perceiver, perceptions, and external objects, as in Plato's cave allegory. He contrasts metaphysical/epistemological realism with idealism and antirealism, deploys the movie-theater picture of solipsism drawn from Hume's bundle of perceptions and Berkeley's denial of the external world, and argues Hetfield's own practice as a songwriter proves he is a realist - while distinguishing healthy philosophical skepticism from the lyric's irrational mistrust.

chapters.file: ch21 - Trapped in Myself One and the Mind-Body Problem.md
chapters.relation: Joanna Corwin reads 'One' - Joe Bonham, a mind fully conscious in a destroyed body, 'Trapped in myself / Body my holding cell' - as the mind-body problem. She walks through Descartes: methodological doubt and the dream argument mirrored in Joe's 'Can't tell if this is true or dream', the cogito as Joe's 'thinking thinking thinking', substance dualism, and the evil-deceiver worry. But Metallica's song also answers Descartes: a disembodied thinking-substance lives a 'life in hell', and Joe's tapping of S-O-S in Morse code shows a mind needs a body to communicate and complete itself.

chapters.file: ch22 - Is It Still Metallica On the Identity of Rock Bands Over Time.md
chapters.relation: Manuel Bremer and Daniel Cohnitz ask whether the band on Kill 'Em All is identical with the band on St. Anger. Lars' drum kit, rebuilt part by part plus the reassembled original, is a Ship of Theseus case yielding their 'Nothing Else Matters Principle'; Locke's distinction between same substance, man, and person - illustrated by a brain swap between Kirk Hammett and an envious rival - shows identity must be 'suited to the idea'; and Searle and Gilbert on collective intention show a band is a social group, not a collection of people. Their revised musical-style-plus-line-up-continuity theory faces fission problems (Megadeth) and the eliminativist option Quine's 'no entity without identity' invites.

chapters.file: ch23 - Fans and the Band.md
ch24 - Metallica Drops a Load What Do Bands and Fans Owe Each Other.md
chapters.relation: Mark White asks whether Metallica wronged its longtime fans by changing style on Load, using Kant's duty ethics. No duty to keep their thrash style survives the categorical imperative - a world where every band changes style is horrible but not contradictory - and Kantian duties to the band members' families, employees, and to their own talents and authenticity actually support the change. Symmetrically, fans' loyalty is only an imperfect duty with wiggle room: it is owed in return for the band's loyalty to its metal values, and lapses when the motivation is mere commercial sell-out.

chapters.file: ch25 - The Unsocial Sociability of Humans and Metal Gods.md
chapters.relation: Niall Scott applies Kant's 'unsocial sociability' - the human oscillation between solitude and society - to Metallica: the ego-clashes of Some Kind of Monster and the Hetfield-Mustaine rivalry ('Better Than You') instantiate Kant's vices of culture, yet produce the music as the reconciliation of the struggle. Using 'The Struggle Within' and 'Hero of the Day', he runs the categorical imperative on refusing help (the maxim cannot be universalized) to ground Kant's imperfect duty of beneficence, and answers Schiller's 'duty with hatred' objection - the 'My Friend of Misery' syndrome - by noting Kant allows feelings to support duty.

chapters.file: ch26 - Boys Interrupted The Drama of Male Bonding in Some Kind of Monster.md
chapters.relation: Judith Grant reads Some Kind of Monster through Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick's concept of homosociality: the Hetfield-Ulrich bond is the libidinal engine of the band, with Mustaine and Newsted as sibling rivals for James' attention, wives and children as intrusions that break the male-only bonding, and Lars' French-kissing of Kirk policing the homosocial/homosexual line within heteronormativity. The film's arc - James' exit to rehab, Lars' tirade against his control, and the firing of the feminized therapist Phil - is the interruption and rekindling of a homosocial bond that can no longer run on youthful rebellion now that the band has become 'The Man'.

chapters.file: ch27 - Justice for All Metallica's Argument Against Napster and Internet File Sharing.md
chapters.relation: Robert Delfino evaluates the Napster lawsuit philosophically: Aristotle's law of non-contradiction exposes Lars Ulrich's inconsistent statements about money and his tolerance of 1980s home taping despite admitting to it, weakening the band's case. But the core argument is consistent and Lockean - Lars' Senate testimony that 'just like a carpenter who crafts a table gets to decide whether to keep it, sell it, or give it away' invokes Locke's labor theory of property, which Delfino defends against Tom Palmer's objection that copyright restricts bodily liberty, distinguishing it from the Constitution's utilitarian rationale for copyright.

holes.name: Homosociality
holes.what: Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick's term for the social bonds between persons of the same sex, which she places on a continuum with homosexuality as forms of desire that structure male bonding and its exclusions.
holes.why: Chapter 26's entire analysis of Some Kind of Monster - the Hetfield-Ulrich bond, the rivalry with Mustaine, the exclusion of women, and the policing of the homosocial/homosexual line - is built on this concept, which taxonomy.json lacks.

holes.name: Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick
holes.what: American queer-theory and gender-studies theorist (1950-2009), author of Between Men and Epistemology of the Closet, who developed the concept of homosocial desire.
holes.why: Chapter 26 explicitly frames its reading of Metallica's male bonding with Sedgwick's account of the homosocial-homosexual continuum, and no taxonomy philosopher covers this framework.
